interviewQuestions.question: How would you design auth for a system with 20 internal services?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd split this into two separate problems: user authentication and service-to-service authentication, because conflating them is the most common mistake here.

For user auth, I'd terminate the expensive credential check once at the API gateway or a dedicated identity service, then issue a short-lived signed token the client attaches to every call. Downstream services verify that token's signature cheaply — no repeated password checks, no shared session lookup on every hop.

For service-to-service calls, I'd add mTLS so each of the 20 services proves its own identity independently of any user, and forward a scoped claim (not the raw user token) alongside it so a service can act on the user's behalf without being able to replay their full credential elsewhere.

I'd close by naming the failure mode this avoids: without service identity, one compromised service can impersonate any other service in the call graph.

**Testing:** whether you separate user identity from service identity instead of solving both with one mechanism.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Auth across 20 internal services

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose token-based auth over session-based auth for a new system?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start from the actual constraint driving the decision, not a default preference. Token-based auth wins when I need many independent services to verify identity without a shared datastore — a JWT's signature can be checked locally by any node, which matters once you're horizontally scaled across services that don't all share one database.

I'd pick session-based auth instead when instant revocation is a hard requirement — banking-style "kill this login the second we suspect fraud" — because deleting one server-side record is immediate, while a valid JWT stays valid until it expires no matter what happens next.

In practice I'd often land on a hybrid: short-lived access tokens for the scaling benefit, paired with a revocable refresh token so I still get a fast kill switch when it matters.

**Testing:** whether you can justify the choice against concrete requirements — revocation speed, scale, shared infrastructure — rather than reciting a definition.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Token vs session, when to choose

interviewQuestions.question: How do you make logout work correctly across many microservices when some of them cache identity locally?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd first ask which auth model is in play, because the answer differs. With session-based auth, logout is straightforward — deleting the central session record makes every service that checks it see the user as logged out immediately.

With tokens, I'd design for the fact that a signed token stays technically valid until it expires. I'd keep access tokens short-lived and pair them with a revocable refresh token, so the blast radius of "still valid after logout" is bounded to minutes, not days. For services that hold their own local cache of a user's identity, I'd add an event — publish "user logged out" and have each service evict its cache — rather than assuming every service will re-check a central source on every request.

I'd close by naming the trade-off explicitly: this is a latency-versus-certainty decision, and I'd pick the bound based on how sensitive the system is to a stale session.

**Testing:** whether you recognize that distributed logout is a design problem, not a one-line database delete.
